title: Honour
paragraphs: Explaining grammar is not my sole objective in this work. It is an attempt at aiding learners of Tolkāppiyam to retain in mind the significant aspects of grammatical norms and principles. As a part of this, I seek to explain here cāriyai (empty morph) which unfolds in the form of a scene.
Wordbooks define aikāram as chest, ornament worn on the shoulder, rebuke, snake, falsehood, elephant’s food, etc.
In the same manner, māṉam means self-respect, haughtiness, pain, guilt, love, affection and chastity.
The grammatical term cāriyai is not only a word of the closed system but also a kind of dance of the puṟam mode.
āṭūu denotes a male and makaṭūu denotes a female.
Bearing these in mind, it would be useful as well as amusing to read this ‘blossom’.
Now, Nallatampi and Nallataṅkai - brother and sister - were taking leave of their parents for staging a dance performance.

A learned Tamil teacher - Cellaiyā, marked with a confused mind, met the siblings on the way. On encountering their parents, the teacher once again enquired, “Where are your children off to?”, completely forgetting his meeting with the children earlier.

“Isn’t today āṭipperukku? The rivers would flow to their fill marking the greatness of the regime. In such a joyous function, which men and women enjoy to the hilt, my son and daughter are going to enjoy themselves by entertaining the people through a dance”, was the explanation offered to the teacher.
“What role are the brother and sister going to play in that dance?”
“Nallatampi would don the role of Kōvalaṉ, while his sister pairs opposite to him as Kōvalaṉ’s mistress Mātavi.”
“Brother and sister playing the characters of Kōvalaṉ and Mātavi?” exclaimed Cellaiyā, the scholar. After a momentary pondering, he commented laughingly, “māṉamillai” meaning ‘dishonourable’.
It was enough to provoke the parents, “Teacher! How dare you say such a defaming and offending word to us!”. The agitated parents lost no time to arm themselves with a sickle and a log.
It sent shivers down the spine of the teacher who muttered, “Why such agitation? Now, what offensive thing did I utter?”
“Then what? You enquired about my children and dismissed them as shameless! How can I tolerate this?”

“Well, I am just returning from the school after teaching Tolkāppiyam to children. Since my mind was still preoccupied with what I taught in the classroom, I stammered something. In retrospect, there is nothing wrong with my remark.”
“What? Is there nothing wrong?”
“Kindly bear with me! Let me offer my explanation first. In Tolkāppiyam’s Eḻuttatikāram there is a verse on cāriyai:
> For the intervening empty morpheme iṉ to occur > After the two preceding terms āṭūu and makaṭūu > [Besides the hard consonant augmentation] > Is no failing in use.

Cāriyai doesn’t mean dance alone; it also refers to morphemes of closed word class. The relevant verse states clearly that in ‘āṭūu’ and ‘makaṭūu’ which refer to man and woman respectively, not only hard consonants but even if cāriyai occurs, it is not wrong.

‘āṭūu’ and ‘makaṭūu’, that is, brother and sister playing the roles of Kōvalaṉ and Mātavi respectively is not erroneous. This is what I wished to state. Māṉam means wrong, māṉam illai means that it is not wrong.”

The parents sighed with relief and looked at the teacher, “Sir, though brother and sister are paired opposite to each other, it is after all a form of art. Therefore, it is not a sin. Didn’t you get a simpler word to express the same opinion? Why did you perplex us by uttering the seemingly offending word ‘māṉam illai’?”
“That is what I am reiterating: in between ‘āṭūu’ and ‘makaṭūu’, not only hard consonants but even if cāriyai appears, it is not a mistake. Since I was engrossed in
what I taught in the classroom, I uttered the word māṉam illai in that sense. This is the cause of all the misunderstanding. My apologies.”
Thus pleasing the parents, the teacher took their leave, with the satisfaction that he was able to throw light on a verse of Tolkāppiyam.

> For the intervening empty morpheme iṉ to occur > After the two preceding terms āṭūu and makaṭūu > [Besides the hard consonant augmentation] > Is no failing in use. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Uyir Mayaṅkiyal, verse 69)
